item.title: Molecular architecture of Cryptococcus cell walls reveals species-specific chitosan-dependent remodeling
item.dc:creator: Ankur Ankur
Rajendra Upadhya
Mahsa Doosti
Davis Ferreira
Sara E. Miller
Li Xie
Ivan Hung
Jennifer K. Lodge
item.description:
Authors: Ankur Ankur, Rajendra Upadhya, Mahsa Doosti, Davis Ferreira, Sara E. Miller, Li Xie, Ivan Hung, Jennifer K. Lodge, et al.
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Cryptococcus neoformans and Cryptococcus gattii are fungal pathogens that cause life-threatening infections, including cryptococcal meningitis. A distinctive feature of the cryptococcal cell wall is the extensive deacetylation of chitin to chitosan, a modification that is essential for virulence but whose structural role in cell-wall organization remains poorly understood. Here, we analyze the cell walls of wild-type strains of both species and their avirulent chitosan-deficient mutants, which serve as vaccine candidates. Loss of chitosan disrupted cell morphology and altered cell-wall ultrastructure, with more pronounced defects in C. neoformans . Solid-state NMR reveals that aggregated α-(1→3)-glucans form the principal rigid domain of the cell wall in both species and are closely associated with chitin microfibrils, whereas surrounding β-glucans and mannoproteins constitute a more dynamic matrix. Chitosan modulates hydration and flexibility, and its loss increases chitin exposure and triggers species-specific remodeling of the polysaccharide network. In C. neoformans , chitosan depletion increased α-(1→3)-glucan content and reduced β-glucan levels, whereas C. gattii selectively lost one α-(1→3)-glucan subtype while maintaining β-glucan levels. Although capsule production remained intact, chitosan deficiency altered glucuronoxylomannan linkage patterns and mannoprotein composition. These findings reveal how chitosan organizes cryptococcal cell-wall architecture and highlight distinct structural adaptation strategies among pathogenic Cryptococcus species.

item.title: Bacteroides–Escherichia interactions contribute to colonization resistance against Clostridioides difficile
item.dc:creator: Achuthan Ambat
Naomi Iris van den Berg
Francisco Zorrilla
Shruti Menon
Abhijit Maji
Tanim Islam
Arianna Basile
Sudeep Ghimire
item.description:
Authors: Achuthan Ambat, Naomi Iris van den Berg, Francisco Zorrilla, Shruti Menon, Abhijit Maji, Tanim Islam, Arianna Basile, Sudeep Ghimire, et al.
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Commensal gut bacteria are key contributors to the resilience against pathogen invasion. This is exemplified by the success of faecal microbiota transplantation in treating recurrent Clostridioides difficile infection. Yet, characteristics of communities that can confer colonisation resistance and the underlying mechanisms remain largely unknown. Here we use a synthetic community of 14 commensal gut bacteria to uncover inter-species interactions and metabolic pathways underpinning the emergent resilience against C. difficile invasion. We challenged this synthetic community as well as faecal-matter-derived communities with antibiotic treatment and C. difficile in a continuous flow bioreactor. Using generalised Lotka-Volterra and genome-scale metabolic modelling, we identified interactions between Escherichia coli and Bacteroides/Phocaeicola sp. as key to the pathogen’s suppression. Metabolomics and targeted validation experiments revealed that fructan-derived fructooligosaccharides, vitamin B3 biosynthesis, and competition for Stickland metabolism precursors causally contribute to suppression across multiple C. difficile strains and donor backgrounds. Analysis of metagenomics data from patient cohorts and clinical trials attested the in vivo relevance of the identified metabolic pathways and the ratio between Bacteroides and Escherichia in successful colonisation resistance. The latter was found to be a stronger discriminator than commonly used alpha diversity metrics. Together, our study uncovers emergent microbial interactions in pathogen resistance with implications for rational design of bacteriotherapies.

item.title: Confining chlorine in the cation solvation sheaths towards stable and sustainable seawater electrolysis
item.dc:creator: Peng-Cheng Yu
Ye-Hua Wang
Xiao-Long Zhang
Shu-Ping Sun
Tao Fang
Xu-Ying-Nan Tao

item.description:
Authors: Peng-Cheng Yu, Ye-Hua Wang, Xiao-Long Zhang, Shu-Ping Sun, Tao Fang, Xu-Ying-Nan Tao, Yu Yang, Jie Liao, et al.
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Chlorine electro-oxidation represents the primary anode side reaction during direct seawater electrolysis, causing corrosion and permanent deactivation of catalyst and thereby insufficient stability. We report that in situ segregated fluorine can actuate the desolvation of cations and Cl − ions via strong H ∙ ∙ ∙ F bonding, leading to the formation of intimate cation-Cl − contact ion pairs that make Cl − migration toward electrode surface prohibited. Meanwhile, fluorine remaining in the cobalt-based catalyst shortens the Co–Co distance, attributable to its large electronegativity, triggering an oxide path mechanism that circumvents the nonideal scaling between OH * and OOH * during oxygen-evolving reaction. Direct seawater electrolysis (with 1 M NaOH) incorporating this catalyst achieves 1 ampere per square centimeter (A cm −2 ) at 1.7 volts and maintains at 0.5 A cm −2 and 60 °C over 2,450 hours degrading at 24.9 microvolts per hour. Our catalyst even survives repeatedly switched current densities (0.25, 0.5, and 1 A cm −2 ) for more than 1,250 hours, manifesting compatibility with fluctuating renewable electricity.

item.title: Low-Dose Glucocorticoids Adjunctive to Flow Diverter Therapy for Unruptured Intracranial Aneurysms Improve Cerebrovascular Outcomes
item.dc:creator: Zhuohua Wen
Xiheng Chen
Xin Tong
Chi Huang
Mengshi Huang
Jiancheng Lin
Anqi Xu
Hanyan Yang
item.description:
Authors: Zhuohua Wen, Xiheng Chen, Xin Tong, Chi Huang, Mengshi Huang, Jiancheng Lin, Anqi Xu, Hanyan Yang, et al.
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Flow diverter (FD) implantation is standard for unruptured intracranial aneurysms (UIAs), but cerebrovascular complications persist. This nested study within a prospective multicenter cohort evaluates whether short-term, low-dose glucocorticoid use is associated with cerebrovascular outcomes after FD implantation. Propensity-score matching with exact matching on UIA location yielded 1327 patients (360 glucocorticoid-treated; 967 controls). Intravenous glucocorticoids, initiated within 2 hours of the FD procedure and administered for ≥2 days, were associated with fewer in-hospital cerebrovascular events (6.9% vs. 13.1%; adjusted odds ratio [aOR], 0.53) and major cerebrovascular events (4.7% vs. 12.4%; aOR, 0.37). Over a median 2-year follow-up, glucocorticoid use was also associated with fewer new-onset major cerebrovascular events (3.6% vs. 8.7%; adjusted hazard ratio, 0.41) and less in-stent stenosis (7.9% vs. 13.2%; aOR, 0.55). Findings remained robust in unmatched patients on sensitivity analyses. We demonstrate that perioperative glucocorticoid regimens may reduce cerebrovascular events and in-stent stenosis in FD-treated patients, warranting randomized trials.

item.title: Rationally micropatterned antifogging hydrogels counteracting extreme condensation
item.dc:creator: Hyunchul Park
Cheuk Wing Edmond Lam
Iwan Haechler
Thomas M. Schutzius
Dimos Poulikakos
item.description:
Authors: Hyunchul Park, Cheuk Wing Edmond Lam, Iwan Haechler, Thomas M. Schutzius, Dimos Poulikakos
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Loss of transparency due to water vapor condensation is a widespread problem across diverse applications such as windows, eyewear, displays, vehicles, and kitchenware. Conventional antifogging strategies relying on hydrophilic or hydrophobic coatings, based on chemistry and/or nano-topography, can counteract up to mild water deposition, but lose functionality at excessive condensation environments. Here, we present a passive approach, rationally micropatterning an inherently hydrophilic hydrogel to maintain high transparency under supersaturation. Guided by optics and wetting theory, and employing a diffusion model to calculate related timescales of water film formation, we engineer a wicking structure on poly(ethylene glycol) diacrylate hydrogel, facilitating long-term sustainable filmwise condensation. Employing quantitative optical clarity measurements and visualization, we show that our approach clearly outperforms state-of-the-art antifogging alternatives, retaining high optical clarity even in boiling environments. Facile fabrication and superior performance establish our microstructured hydrogel as an excellent choice for sustaining transparency under extreme condensation.

item.title: Baseline radiographic and microbiologic predictors of treatment outcomes in a shortened all-oral regimen for MDR/RR-TB
item.dc:creator: Edmund Q. L. Shen
Stephane Mpinda
Llang Maama
Meseret Tamirat
Phate Sebakeng
Lawrence Oyewusi
Allison LaHood
Letizia Trevisi
item.description:
Authors: Edmund Q. L. Shen, Stephane Mpinda, Llang Maama, Meseret Tamirat, Phate Sebakeng, Lawrence Oyewusi, Allison LaHood, Letizia Trevisi, et al.
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract WHO-endorsed shortened, all-oral regimens have improved tolerability and outcomes for MDR/RR-TB treatment, but predictors of poor outcomes remain incompletely-characterized. We conducted a prospective cohort study (NCT05871489) of adults with bacteriologically-confirmed pulmonary MDR/RR-TB treated with a shortened, all-oral regimen in Lesotho. We evaluated baseline microbiologic and radiographic features and their associations with time-to-culture-conversion, end-of-treatment outcomes, and final post-treatment outcomes. Among 238 participants (median age 41 [IQR:31–56], 29% female, 62% with HIV), there were 27 unfavorable outcomes (20 deaths, 3 treatment failures, 4 recurrences). 142 of 148 (95.9%) with positive baseline cultures experienced conversion within four months. Fibrosis, cavitation, bilateral disease, and high smear grade were associated with delayed culture conversion and lower odds of treatment success. Bilateral disease was more strongly associated with unfavorable outcomes in those without HIV; fibrosis and high smear grade showed stronger associations among those with HIV. Cavitation with high smear grade (uOR=0.29, 95%CI:0.11–0.78; aOR=0.39, 95%CI:0.14-1.14), and severe fibrocavitary disease (multi-lobar fibrosis and at least one cavity ≥5 cm) (uOR=0.20, 95%CI:0.07–0.64; aOR=0.26, 95%CI:0.07-0.94) were negatively associated with favorable final outcomes. These findings suggest that baseline sputum and chest radiographic features—particularly in-combination—identify higher-risk patients and may inform risk-adapted strategies for shortened all-oral MDR/RR-TB regimens.

item.title: Nonflammable sulfamoyl–carbonate hybrid electrolyte for high-voltage lithium batteries via preemptive passivation
item.dc:creator: Hun Kim
Jae-Min Kim
Yo-Han Yang
Xiaosheng Song
Dong-Gun Koo
Kang Xu
Yang-Kook Sun
item.description:
Authors: Hun Kim, Jae-Min Kim, Yo-Han Yang, Xiaosheng Song, Dong-Gun Koo, Kang Xu, Yang-Kook Sun
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Achieving high energy density without compromising safety remains a significant challenge for advanced batteries. Nonflammable electrolytes can mitigate fire risk, but poor bulk and interfacial properties of such electrolytes limit their application. Here, a nonflammable sulfamoyl–carbonate electrolyte was developed, achieving a self-extinguishing time of ~0 s and stable cycling in both lithium metal and lithium-ion batteries under high-voltage conditions. The electrolyte comprising lithium hexafluorophosphate dissolved in dimethylsulfamoyl fluoride, fluoroethylene carbonate, and ethyl methyl carbonate at low concentration establishes a weakly solvating environment, wherein dimethylsulfamoyl fluoride and fluoroethylene carbonate preferentially contribute to stabilize the positive and negative electrodes, while working together to enhance the rate capability, low-temperature performance, and long-term cycling at high-voltage. Accelerating rate calorimetry revealed a delayed thermal runaway onset by 87 °C, correlating with Broadness Index. These findings suggest that preemptive passivation on both electrodes, when coupled with nonflammable electrolyte design, can provide a viable route toward safe, high-energy lithium batteries.

item.title: Coordinated control of both microtubule ends regulates mitotic spindle length
item.dc:creator: Shane A. Fiorenza
Sheba Cheeran
Elena Doria
Iva M. Tolić
Patrick Meraldi
Nenad Pavin
item.description:
Authors: Shane A. Fiorenza, Sheba Cheeran, Elena Doria, Iva M. Tolić, Patrick Meraldi, Nenad Pavin
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract The mitotic spindle is a biomechanical structure whose length must be precisely controlled to ensure faithful chromosome segregation. The treadmilling of microtubules towards spindle poles, termed poleward flux, is involved in spindle length control. However, poleward flux velocity has been shown to be both inversely and directly proportional to spindle length, a contradiction that remains unexplained by current mechanisms. Here we introduce a model which demonstrates that length-dependent regulation at both microtubule ends allows plus- and minus-end dynamics to synchronize with one another, enabling pathways of poleward-flux-based spindle length control which rectify previous results. Moreover, our model predicts that spindle length and poleward flux velocity can vary independently via simultaneous perturbations at both microtubule ends, which we validate with protein depletion experiments in human cells. Finally, we provide experimental evidence for length-dependent accumulation of proteins at microtubule minus-ends. Our results thus resolve a longstanding paradox and provide mechanistic insight into the reciprocal control of spindle length and poleward flux.

item.title: A CRC–MYB chromatin loop controls auxin-mediated nectary growth in Arabidopsis
item.dc:creator: Hideaki Iimura
Makoto Takahashi
Ryosuke Ohta
Asumi Nagamori
Seika Togawa
Yuki Furuta
Koki Nakamura
Febri Yuda Kurniawan
item.description:
Authors: Hideaki Iimura, Makoto Takahashi, Ryosuke Ohta, Asumi Nagamori, Seika Togawa, Yuki Furuta, Koki Nakamura, Febri Yuda Kurniawan, et al.
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Floral nectaries, typically located at stamen bases, secrete sugar-rich nectar containing diverse secondary metabolites. Despite their defined position and specialized function, the mechanisms governing nectary formation remain unclear. Using publicly available single-nucleus RNA-seq data and newly generated spatial transcriptomic data, we identify a putative ordering of transcriptional states associated with nectary development and a spatial regulatory network controlling nectary growth in Arabidopsis thaliana . We further show that CRABS CLAW (CRC) is central to this network, integrating transcriptional regulation with spatial auxin transport and pathways controlling phytohormone signaling, sugar transport and terpene biosynthesis. CRC interacts with MYB21, MYB24 and MYB57 to form a complex that binds the 5′ and 3′ regulatory regions of MACCHI-BOU 4 ( MAB4 ), promoting a chromatin loop that enhances MAB4 expression and supports proper nectary size. MAB4 reinforces PIN-FORMED 1-mediated auxin transport to establish auxin maxima at the nectary tip and regulates PIN6 localization to maintain auxin gradients. These findings link transcriptional regulation and auxin transport with nectary organogenesis and metabolic function.

item.title: Spatially resolving isomeric trisaccharides on surfaces with Orbitrap-SIMS
item.dc:creator: Margaret Moloney
Richard Paterson
Bin Yan
Anya Eyres
Clare L. Newell
Jean-Luc Vorng
Alexander Pirkl
John F. Watts
item.description:
Authors: Margaret Moloney, Richard Paterson, Bin Yan, Anya Eyres, Clare L. Newell, Jean-Luc Vorng, Alexander Pirkl, John F. Watts, et al.
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Many biologically important molecules are structural isomers that share the same molecular mass yet differ in shape, bonding and function. This creates an ambiguity for mass spectrometry imaging (MSI), where chemically distinct species can be indistinguishable on the mass-to-charge ( m/z) scale and therefore cannot be reliably mapped in heterogeneous materials. Here we demonstrate that Orbitrap secondary ion mass spectrometry (OrbiSIMS) can provide an orthogonal contrast that enables both identification and spatial separation of isomeric molecules directly on surfaces. By exploiting structure-dependent secondary-ion dissociation and gas-phase collisional effects during ion transmission, we discriminate isomeric trisaccharides raffinose, maltotriose and melezitose and spatially resolve raffinose and maltotriose in mixtures. We benchmark these measurements against ion mobility spectrometry and observe consistent trends between OrbiSIMS transmission behaviour and ion mobility separation. These results establish OrbiSIMS as an approach for isomer-resolved MSI at surfaces and interfaces, opening opportunities to map isomeric biomolecules in complex systems where spatial distribution is central to function.

item.title: Accounting for longitudinal peak quality metrics with MSstats+ enhances differential analysis in proteomic experiments with data-independent acquisition
item.dc:creator: Devon Kohler
Eralp Dogu
Mrittika Bhattacharya
Ozge Karayel
Manuel Magana
Anthony Wu
Veronica G. Anania
Olga Vitek
item.description:
Authors: Devon Kohler, Eralp Dogu, Mrittika Bhattacharya, Ozge Karayel, Manuel Magana, Anthony Wu, Veronica G. Anania, Olga Vitek
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Mass spectrometry-based proteomics with data-independent acquisition benefits from advanced instrumentation and computational analysis. Despite continued improvements, the quality of quantification may be poor for some measurements. As the scale of proteomic experiments increases, these poor-quality measurements are challenging to characterize by hand, yet they undermine the detection of differentially abundant proteins and the downstream biological conclusions. We introduce MSstats + , a computational workflow that takes as input not only peak intensities reported by tools such as Spectronaut or DIA-NN, but also quality metrics such as peak shape and retention time, and longitudinal run order profiles of these metrics. MSstats+ translates these metrics into a single measure of quality, and downweights poor quality measurements when detecting differentially abundant proteins. The method offers a natural treatment of missing values, weighting the imputed values according to the quality metrics in the run. We demonstrate the accuracy of the resulting differential analysis in five experiments: two custom benchmarking studies with intentionally induced anomalies, a controlled mixture of proteomes, and two large-scale clinical investigations. MSstats+ is implemented in the family of open-source R/Bioconductor packages MSstats.

item.title: Developing and benchmarking one health genomic surveillance tools for influenza A virus in wastewater
item.dc:creator: Minxi Jiang
Audrey L. W. Wang
James B. Thissen
Kara L. Nelson
Lenore Pipes
Rose S. Kantor
item.description:
Authors: Minxi Jiang, Audrey L. W. Wang, James B. Thissen, Kara L. Nelson, Lenore Pipes, Rose S. Kantor
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Influenza A viruses (IAV) remain a persistent One Health threat, and whole-genome sequencing from wastewater offers a promising surveillance tool. However, IAV is at low abundance in wastewater, making it difficult to sequence. We benchmark four targeted enrichment methods suited for multi-subtype whole-genome IAV sequencing including custom and off-the-shelf methods. Our custom HA tiled-amplicon panel is sensitive, fast, and cost-effective, making it suitable for monitoring low-abundance seasonal variants of known subtypes, although its reliance on conserved and intact primer-binding sites limits primer design to fewer subtypes. A published universal amplicon method targets all IAV subtypes but performs poorly in wastewater due to its reliance on intact genome segments. Meanwhile, probe-capture methods are resilient to RNA degradation. In real wastewater samples, our custom probe panel recovers whole-genome signals from circulating H1N1, H3N2, H5N1, including validated H5N1 2.3.4.4b reads in samples where dPCR detection is limited. However, probe-capture is generally more costly and labor-intensive than amplicon methods. Across all four sequencing methods, two wastewater matrices, and most spike-in and endogenous virus targets, ultrafiltration-based virus concentration consistently outperforms large-volume direct extraction. Together, these benchmarking comparisons and custom panels provide needed information for implementing IAV genomic sequencing in routine wastewater surveillance.

item.title: Breaking water-structure constraints by Hofmeister effects in interfacial polymerization for polyamide membranes
item.dc:creator: Qingchen Tang
Hao Chen
Yu Chen
Hanyu Wu
Xingwang Meng
Wu Jin
Panjia Jiang
Yizhou Zhang
item.description:
Authors: Qingchen Tang, Hao Chen, Yu Chen, Hanyu Wu, Xingwang Meng, Wu Jin, Panjia Jiang, Yizhou Zhang, et al.
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Hydration critically governs the physicochemical behavior of solutes in both the aqueous bulk and interfacial environments. As typical chaotropic Hofmeister ions, weakly hydrated anions (WHAs) can reshape hydration structures and accumulate at water–hydrophobe interfaces. Notably, WHAs paradoxically suppress the solubility of certain small-molecule monomers in water while enhancing that of chemically analogous polymers. Here, we exploit WHA-mediated Hofmeister hydration control to regulate polyamide-forming interfacial polymerization (IP), using the piperazine (PIP) and trimesoyl chloride (TMC) nanofiltration system as the primary model. Introducing WHAs into the aqueous phase reduces the affinity of amine monomers for water and accelerates partitioning into the reaction front in the oil phase, remarkably reinforcing IP self-limitation. Simultaneously, interfacial WHA enrichment lowers interfacial tension and, together with accelerated amine delivery, potentially intensifies transport-driven interfacial instabilities. WHAs also lower interfacial water availability, attenuating acyl chloride hydrolysis. These synergistic effects yield hollow-ridged polyamide selective layers with reduced thickness and high crosslinking density, delivering enhanced water permeance and salt rejection. Crucially, module-scale fabrication of high-performance membranes demonstrates that WHA-mediated Hofmeister hydration control is directly compatible with established desalination pipelines.

Abstract: Abstract The GID/CTLH family of E3 ubiquitin ligases employs several substrate receptor subunits that recruit distinct degrons, but the substrate recognition mechanisms of the CTLH MKLN1 assembly have largely remained elusive. item.dc:creator: Mitchell Dickau
H. Damon Matthews
item.description:
Authors: Mitchell Dickau, H. Damon Matthews
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Carbon removal and storage is central to many net-zero commitments, yet its durability, particularly for nature-based methods, is uncertain due to disturbance risks. Previous work shows that carbon storage-years (the time-integrated quantity of carbon storage) are proportional to time-integrated avoided warming, which in turn causes avoided changes in slow-responding climate variables. Here, we show that temporary carbon storage results in avoided changes in inertial climate variables. Avoided changes in 2100 are proportional to carbon storage-years across a range of storage amounts and emissions scenarios for permafrost carbon, ocean carbon, Atlantic meridional overturning circulation, ocean temperature, and thermosteric sea-level rise. By 2300, proportionality persists in some variables, notably sea-level rise, ocean temperature, and ocean carbon. Temporary storage therefore has climate benefits that extend beyond the duration of the storage, with some persistence of benefits even on multi-century timescales. We find that these climate benefits are greatest when temporary storage is paired with ambitious mitigation.

Authors: Satya Prakash, Clenira Varela, Mark Walsh, Roberto Galizi, Mark Isalan, Alfonso Jaramillo
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Training physical neural networks directly in matter remains difficult because most platforms do not store and update weights within the same physical substrate. Here we show that engineered Escherichia coli can implement a genetically encoded local learning rule acting on persistent biological memory. We introduce memregulons: bacterial memory elements in which coupled plasmids store an analogue weight as the relative abundance of P1 within the P1 + P2 plasmid pool. Environmental inputs activate local promoters, and a shared sublethal kanamycin signal converts promoter activity into differential growth that lowers the stored P1 fraction. Across single-strain trajectories, combined plate-reader and flow-cytometry measurements are consistent with activity- and variance-dependent weight change. At the single-cell level, repeated negative learning reshapes the stored weight distribution as it approaches the lower boundary. In mixed populations and co-cultures, one shared negative learning signal selectively rewrites active memregulons, enabling externally routed supervised tic-tac-toe lessons. We then generalise the architecture across orthogonal chemical inputs and combinatorial promoters, and combine measured co-culture updates with external game analysis and simulate negative pruning in nonlinear-classifier architectures. These results establish physical learning in living matter through local negative updates of genetically encoded analogue weights.

Abstract: Abstract To protect themselves against phage infection, bacteria employ diverse defense systems that are typically activated specifically upon infection. Authors: Yanan Zhu, Juan S. Rey, Juan Shen, Juan R. Perilla, Peijun Zhang
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract The HIV-1 capsid, composed of capsid (CA) proteins arranged into a conical surface lattice, serves as a critical platform for host–pathogen interactions. Many host cofactors regulate HIV-1 infection by selectively recognizing the higher-order CA lattice rather than individual monomers or capsomers. Among these, Myxovirus resistance protein B (MxB) is a key cellular restriction factor that binds the capsid via its N-terminal fragment containing an arginine-rich motif (RRR), blocking HIV-1 infection at early infection stages. However, the structural basis of this interaction has remained elusive. Here, we present a structural characterization of the CA lattice in complex with the MxB N-terminal fragment using cryo-electron tomography and subtomogram averaging. Combining cryoEM structures with EM-guided all-atom molecular dynamics simulations, we identify residue-specific interactions between MxB and the CA trimer interfaces. Notably, residues 10-20 of the MxB N-terminus adopt an α-helical conformation that stabilizes binding at the CA trimer interface, revealing a distinct mode of capsid engagement. These findings provide insight into arginine-rich motif–mediated recognition by MxB and other host factors and establish a structural framework for the development of capsid-targeting antiviral therapeutics.

Journal: Nature Communications; Volume: 17; Issue: 1; Article number: 10876
Abstract: Abstract Despite significant climate variability in the Northern Hemisphere ~50,000–12,000 years ago, the potential for vertebrates to periodically thrive in the glacial Arctic Ocean has been largely overlooked because ecosystem productivity was assumed to be too low. Here, we analyze fish otoliths preserved in deep-sea sediments and find that two Arctic endemic cod species, ice cod ( Arctogadus glacialis ) and polar cod ( Boreogadus saida ), lived at 87–89 °N ~ 48,000–35,000 years ago and reappeared at the onset of the Holocene ~12,000 years ago. These findings suggest that the glacial Arctic Ocean was not a barren ice desert but rather a breeding ground for the evolution of cold adaptation in marine fish.

Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) remains a major unmet clinical challenge. These findings identify cardiac macrophage signaling rewiring as a central mechanism linking hypertensive stress to metabolic remodeling and inflammation, revealing a pathogenic pathway for HFpEF in the absence of obesity that is distinct from HFpEF associated with obesity.

Abstract: Abstract Representation learning in genomics often relies on sequence, expression, and network data, thereby overlooking a wealth of insights in the scientific literature. Mechanistically, ITLN1 activates a JAK1/STAT3-associated C/EBPδ program that drives terminal granulopoiesis and CXCR2-dependent tumor homing, while recombinant ITLN1 restores neutrophil maturation and tumor-killing activity. Here, we reveal a cross-tissue ITLN1–STAT3/C/EBPδ–CXCR2 axis that links epithelial ITLN1 to bone marrow granulopoiesis, coordinating distal neutrophil maturation, mobilization and spatial organization in colorectal cancer.

Abstract: Abstract Enhanced geothermal systems can provide constant, reliable electricity and heat with minimal emissions, but high drilling costs and uncertain cost reductions leave their future unclear. Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Understanding how global change reshapes species distributions remains a central challenge in ecology, yet most global assessments treat environmental drivers as static, uniform, or aggregate influences. This obscures where, why, and how specific drivers generate ecological risk or opportunity. Here, we apply explainable machine learning to assess how climate averages, variability, extremes, and land cover are projected to reshape future distributions of 1,992 terrestrial mammals. Using Shapley Additive Explanations with species distribution models, we quantify the directional contribution of 16 environmental drivers and track how these contributions change over space and time. We show that climate extremes impose intense but spatially restricted impacts, temperature-related drivers dominate exposure patterns, particularly for specialist species, and the same driver can impose risk in one region while creating opportunity in another. By decomposing projected biodiversity change into driver-specific signatures, our framework advances biodiversity forecasting toward a more actionable understanding of ecological risk and opportunity.

Authors: Qi Huang, Simon Astley, Nikita Rog, Boon Kee Voon, Tushar Singh Verma, Wenyu Shen, Ruixue Sun, Wai Fen Yong, et al.
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Reversible light-driven adsorption in framework materials offers a route to energy-efficient separations, yet current mechanisms deliver modest working capacities that constrain practical utility. Here we introduce photo-reversible defect complexation as a design principle for enhancing light-induced working capacities, coupling photoswitch isomerisation to active binding site modulation rather than pore geometry changes alone. We exploit coordinatively unsaturated Zr sites in defective UiO-67 as reversible binding sites, where a grafted spiropyran (SP) photoswitch undergoes UV-induced isomerisation to the zwitterionic merocyanine (MC) form, whose phenolate oxygen coordinates an additional open Zr site, suppressing guest binding availability. Visible light fully reverses this process. This mechanism delivers an 83% enhancement in photo-modulated CO 2 working capacity, reaching 1.1 mmol g −1 , nearly double that of the structural analog of P-UiO that does not enable photo-reversible MC-defect switching. Light-controlled metal cation and CO 2 uptake confirms that binding site availability, rather than pore geometry, drives this switching response. Density functional theory (DFT) simulations and multimodal X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) confirm reversible MC-Zr site complexation as the operative mechanism with performance retained across multiple photocycles. These findings establish photo-reversible defect engineering as a robust and broadly applicable principle for light-responsive frameworks with modulable guest adsorption.

Journal: Nature Communications; Volume: 17; Issue: 1; Article number: 10872
Abstract: Abstract Understanding the functional consequences of genetic variants, particularly those classified as variants of uncertain significance (VUS), is a major challenge in genomics. While variant effects at protein level are well recognized, roles in post-transcriptional regulation are increasingly appreciated. Here, we introduce cPRIME (prime editing with cDNA readout), a scalable method for assessing variant effects at RNA level. cPRIME employs prime editing to insert genetic variants into endogenous genomic loci, followed by the quantification of changes in variant frequencies at RNA (cDNA) and genomic DNA (gDNA) level. We demonstrate its effectiveness across diverse karyotypes and genomic loci and reveal that synonymous marker edits - frequently used in prime editing screens - can themselves alter RNA processing and thereby confound the interpretation of variant effects. Taken together, cPRIME provides a platform for studying the post-transcriptional consequences of genetic variants in their genomic context and establishes a framework for the functional interpretation of RNA-altering variants in cancer and other diseases.

Abstract: Abstract Pests pose escalating threats to forest ecosystem services globally, yet the patterns of forest vulnerability to these threats remain unclear. Leveraging over 7 million occurrence records of 1875 pest species, we identify northwestern Europe and eastern North America as global epicenters of forest-pest richness, dominated by insect fauna. Abstract: Abstract Natural products are of substantial value in drug discovery screening campaigns. Their three-dimensional structures exhibit high complementarity with target proteins, via a multimodal combination of hydrogen bonds, hydrophobic contacts, electrostatic interactions, and van der Waals interactions. Abstract: Abstract Tectonic deformation on stagnant-lid planets reflects the interaction between long-lived lithospheric structures and evolving stress fields.
